mcqs.question: A team runs a steady, predictable baseline load 24/7 with occasional unpredictable bursts. Which pricing approach fits best?
options: Reserved instances (or a savings plan) covering the steady baseline, with on-demand or spot covering the bursts
All on-demand, since it requires no upfront commitment
All spot instances, since spot is always the cheapest option available
All reserved instances, sized for the peak burst level so nothing ever runs on-demand
mcqs.explanation: Covering the predictable baseline with a reservation captures the discount without sacrificing burst flexibility. All-spot risks reclamation on load that can't tolerate interruption; all-reserved-at-peak pays for unused headroom most of the time; all on-demand forfeits a discount that's available for zero extra risk on the predictable part.

mcqs.question: Why does data egress often cause bigger bill surprises than an idle VM?
options: Egress is disabled by default on every major cloud provider, so it can never be the cause
Egress is billed per GB and scales invisibly with data volume, while a single idle VM has a small, capped hourly cost
Cloud providers never charge for any form of data transfer
An idle VM always costs more per hour than any realistic egress charge
mcqs.explanation: Egress cost scales with volume moved, so a new high-volume job can silently rack up thousands of dollars, whereas an idle VM's hourly rate is small and bounded. Providers do charge for egress by default; it just doesn't show up as one dramatic line item.

mcqs.question: A company gives each team a budget that is actually debited for the cloud resources that team provisions. This is best described as:
options: Showback, because the team can see its usage report
Tagging, because the resources are labeled by team
Chargeback, because the cost has a real budget consequence for the team
A savings plan, because it commits to future spend
mcqs.explanation: Chargeback is defined by an actual billing/budget consequence, not just visibility. Showback only shows the number; tagging is the attribution mechanism underneath both; a savings plan is a pricing commitment, unrelated to who's billed internally.

mcqs.question: A team plans to defer tagging until cost becomes a visible problem. What's the main risk?
options: Tagging retroactively is trivial and free, so there is no real risk
Untagged resources are automatically deleted by most providers after 30 days
Tags only affect which currency the bill is displayed in, not attribution
By the time cost is a problem, many untagged resources already exist and must be traced back to an owner one by one, far slower than tagging at creation time
mcqs.explanation: The cost of deferring tagging is retroactive archaeology across every untagged resource once spend is already a fire to put out. Tagging is cheap at creation and expensive after the fact — the opposite of the assumption in the wrong belief.
